subject: Lockbox request & SKU sizing playbook for reserved-commit sensitivity
messages:
From: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwood.com>
To: Sarah Jones <sarah.jones@lunahealth.com>
Cc: Tim Reed <tim.reed@procureops.com>
Date: Thu, 29 Apr 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Reserved commit sizing proposal and lockbox option

Hi Sarah / Tim,

Thanks again for the time yesterday — per our conversation attached is a short sizing playbook and a first-pass reserved capacity proposal tied to LunaHealth's projected peak routing for Q3–Q4. Key asks / notes: 

- We modeled three SKU buckets (base, burst, overage) to match your expected inference mix. See the attached commit-sizing-diagram.png.
- You asked for an option that reduces exposure to near-term GPU price shocks; the attached GPU_pricing_grid.xlsx includes two protective constructs: a lockbox (partial credit reserve) and a seasonal buffer credit.
- Our standard approach is phased activation (30/45/25% over the first three months) to limit upfront provisioning.

If you'd like, we can route a lockbox escrow for the committed portion, with conditional credits back to LunaHealth if realized spot-like GPU pricing falls below the index floor we set. Does that align with your procurement team's expectations?

I've cc'd Tim from ProcureOps to keep the procurement path aligned. Next step: if LunaHealth is comfortable with the sizing buckets and lockbox concept we'll circulate a short term-sheet and a DocuSign stub.

Best,
Sean
Sr. Account Exec, Redwood Inference
Mobile: +1 415-555-0184

From: Sarah Jones <sarah.jones@lunahealth.com>

Cc: Tim Reed <tim.reed@procureops.com>
Date: Thu, 29 Apr 2027 11:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Reserved commit sizing proposal and lockbox option

Sean — thanks for the materials. Quick reactions from our side: 

1) The SKU buckets look sensible; the phased activation helps our capital planning.
2) Major ask: we need protection vs. a GPU-price collapse. Our finance team will not sign unconstrained commit exposure. The lockbox idea sounds promising — we prefer a third-party escrow or an on-platform credit account that releases only when the index triggers.
3) Can you show a worked example: if GPU market pricing drops 25% in month two, what credit does LunaHealth receive and how does it reconcile against committed usage?

Procurement will also want a short list of acceptance triggers (latency SLOs, throughput minimums) that must be met to avoid discounts being clawed back.

cc: Tim — can you push this through procurement channels?

—Sarah
Head of Product Ops, LunaHealth

- They will hold back signature without a defined reconciliation workflow.

Requesting: Marcus — can finance run a worked example (cost on our side vs. credit obligation) and propose a templated lockbox mechanism? From: Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.com>
To: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Cc: Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.com>, Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.com>, Sarah Jones <sarah.jones@lunahealth.com>
Date: Fri, 30 Apr 2027 08:45:00 -07:00
Subject: RE: Fwd: Reserved commit sizing proposal and lockbox option — LunaHealth asks

Sean / team / Sarah — taking a pass at a commercial construct. High-level:

- Proposal: 12-month reserved commit with a 10% on-signing credit and a 5% locked escrow (third-party custodian or Redwood-managed locked account). Escrow is refundable to customer if the realized weighted GPU index for the quarter falls >15% below the baseline index in our pricing grid.
- Worked example (summary): Commit $600k annualized. If in Q2 GPU index drops 25% vs baseline, we would credit LunaHealth 50% of the escrowed amount back as a one-time billing credit (netting vs future invoices) and then reopen a repricing conversation for subsequent quarters. The spreadsheet includes line-by-line math.
- SKU sizing: keep base/burst/overage buckets. We recommend a phased activation but require a minimum baseline throughput (70% of committed base) for the first 60 days to qualify for any escrow refund. This is to avoid customers signing then not using capacity and then claiming credits.

Conditions for approval: finance can approve up to a 12% effective discount if escrow and monitoring are enabled; anything above requires CRO sign-off. Marcus attached a pricing grid and the worked example.

Next steps: if Luna accepts the escrow mechanics, Olga can draft a short escrow addendum and we circulate a DocuSign stub.

Thanks,
Marcus Lin
Head of Finance, Redwood Inference
[Attachment: GPU_pricing_grid.xlsx (spreadsheet)]

Subject: Re: RE: Fwd: Reserved commit sizing proposal and lockbox option — LunaHealth asks

Marcus — draft looks reasonable from a commercial standpoint. A few legal asks before we send to customer: 

1) Escrow mechanics: specify the third-party custodian, exact trigger calculation (weighted average of our published GPU index across the quarter), and dispute resolution window (30 days).
2) Usage baseline: replace '70% of committed base' with '70% of daily rolling median usage across the 60-day window' — clearer metric for ops.
3) Add monitoring telemetry access: Luna needs read-only access to the billing/usage dashboard for reconciliation.

If finance confirms the 12% approval cap, legal can prepare an escrow addendum template and a short SLO exhibit. Otherwise we need CRO sign-off per Marcus's note.

Olga Petrov
Sr. Counsel, Redwood Inference

Quick update: finance has signed off on a capped commercial (12% max effective discount) if we implement the escrow lockbox + monitoring + the revised usage baseline. I confirmed with our FP&A lead that the worked example keeps downside to Redwood manageable under the 25% market-drop scenario.

Action items for customer-facing doc:
- Olga to draft escrow addendum with explicit trigger math and 30-day dispute window.
- Grace to add a small SLO exhibit (latency P90, error budget) to the short-term sheet.
- Sean to push the DocuSign stub to LunaHealth and track ProcureOps intake.

Sarah — happy to run a 15-minute walkthrough of the worked example and the monitoring dashboard if you want to lock this down this week.

Marcus Lin
